course.title: AP World History: Modern
course.description: Understand the people, ideas, and connections that shaped the world from c. 1200 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Explore how states rose, belief systems spread, trade networks connected regions, and revolutions reshaped societies from c. 1200 to the present.

unit.title: Transoceanic Interconnections
unit.description: Study how new maritime technology, state-sponsored voyages, the Columbian Exchange, and coerced labor connected the world's oceans and reshaped societies.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 4.4 key concept: Europeans established new trading posts in Africa and Asia, which proved profitable for the rulers and merchants involved in new global trade networks
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing the Portuguese trading-post empire, 1498–1600
stimulusBlocks.text:
The Portuguese did not conquer large territories in Asia. Instead they seized fortified ports at key points: Goa in India in 1510, Malacca in 1511, and Hormuz near the Persian Gulf. From these bases they required Asian merchant ships to buy a pass, the cartaz, and pay duties at Portuguese ports, or risk being attacked.

This system brought large profits but limited control. Most Indian Ocean trade continued to be carried by Asian merchants, and powerful land empires such as the Mughals were largely unaffected by Portuguese naval power.

questions.explanation: The author says it brought large profits but limited control.
choiceExplanations: Most trade stayed with Asian merchants.

The author says it brought large profits but limited control.
questions.distinguisher: The author says most trade stayed in Asian hands, so control was far from complete.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 4.4 key concept: European merchants' role in Asian trade was characterized by joint-stock companies and by efforts to dominate trade in specific goods
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing the Dutch East India Company, 1602–1700
stimulusBlocks.text:
In 1602 the Dutch government chartered the Dutch East India Company, known by its Dutch initials VOC. As a joint-stock company, it raised money by selling shares to many investors, who shared the profits and the risks of long, dangerous voyages. The company could build forts, keep soldiers, and make treaties.

From its headquarters at Batavia on Java, founded in 1619, the VOC used force to control the trade in nutmeg, cloves, and mace. On the Banda Islands in the 1620s, company forces killed or enslaved much of the population and replaced them with plantations worked by enslaved laborers.

questions.prompt: The events on the Banda Islands described in the passage show that the VOC

questions.explanation: Company forces killed or enslaved much of the population to control nutmeg.
choiceExplanations: The passage describes force.
The company's goal was profit.
Banda's own population was attacked.
Company forces killed or enslaved much of the population to control nutmeg.
questions.distinguisher: The VOC fought European rivals, but on Banda its violence fell on the islands' own people.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 4.4 key concept: expansion of maritime trading networks fostered the growth of states in Africa, including the Asante and the Kingdom of the Kongo
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing how Kongo and Asante took part in Atlantic trade, c. 1490–1750
stimulusBlocks.text:
The Kingdom of Kongo in west-central Africa established relations with Portugal in the 1480s. King Afonso I, who ruled from about 1509 to 1542, converted to Christianity and exchanged ambassadors with Portugal, but he also wrote letters protesting that Portuguese traders were enslaving his subjects.

The Asante kingdom, which rose in the forests of present-day Ghana around 1700, grew powerful by selling gold and enslaved war captives to European traders on the coast in exchange for firearms and cloth. Its rulers used the firearms to expand their state.

questions.distinguisher: Trade did affect both: Kongo lost subjects to slave raiding and Asante used firearms to expand.

questions.prompt: Which claim does Smith make about the effects of European voyages on the peoples of the Americas and Asia?
choices: Commerce brought peoples of the East and West Indies a lasting improvement in their lives
The benefits of commerce were swallowed up by the injustices Europeans committed
Local rulers successfully resisted European power in remote lands
European governments punished the injustices committed by their traders
questions.explanation: Smith says the benefits of commerce were “sunk and lost” in the misfortunes the discoveries caused for native peoples.
choiceExplanations: Smith says the opposite: any benefits were lost in the misfortunes.
Smith says the benefits of commerce were “sunk and lost” in the misfortunes the discoveries caused for native peoples.
Smith says European superiority of force let them act with impunity.
Smith says Europeans acted with impunity, so nothing suggests punishment.
questions.distinguisher: Smith grants that commerce had a beneficial tendency in general, but he denies that native peoples shared the benefit.

stimulusBlocks.attribution: Adam Smith, Scottish philosopher and economist, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, 1776
stimulusBlocks.citation: Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book IV, ch. 7, part 3. Project Gutenberg eBook #3300.
stimulusBlocks.note: The East Indies and West Indies mean South and Southeast Asia and the Americas. The mercantile system is mercantilism, which Smith criticized.
stimulusBlocks.text:
The discovery of America, and that of a passage to the East Indies by the Cape of Good Hope, are the two greatest and most important events recorded in the history of mankind. . . . By uniting in some measure the most distant parts of the world, by enabling them to relieve one another's wants, to increase one another's enjoyments, and to encourage one another's industry, their general tendency would seem to be beneficial. To the natives, however, both of the East and West Indies, all the commercial benefits which can have resulted from those events have been sunk and lost in the dreadful misfortunes which they have occasioned. . . . At the particular time when these discoveries were made, the superiority of force happened to be so great on the side of the Europeans, that they were enabled to commit with impunity every sort of injustice in those remote countries.

In the mean time, one of the principal effects of those discoveries has been, to raise the mercantile system to a degree of splendour and glory which it could never otherwise have attained to.

questions.prompt: Smith's criticism of the “mercantile system” is best understood in the context of
choices: Protestant arguments against the sale of indulgences in Germany

questions.explanation: Writing in 1776, Smith belonged to the Enlightenment tradition that questioned state control of trade.
choiceExplanations: Arguments over indulgences concerned the Church and belonged to the 1500s.
Defenders of the encomienda argued for forced labor, not for freer trade.
Writing in 1776, Smith belonged to the Enlightenment tradition that questioned state control of trade.
Smith was writing about European economic policy, not Mughal taxation.
questions.distinguisher: Smith wrote about colonial trade, but his critique was of European monopoly policy, not of Spanish labor systems.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 4.4 key concept: joint-stock companies such as the Dutch East India Company combined private investment with state backing
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing the Dutch East India Company, 1602–1700
stimulusBlocks.text:
In 1602 Dutch merchants combined several trading firms into the Dutch East India Company (VOC), which the Dutch government chartered with a monopoly over Dutch trade east of the Cape of Good Hope. The company raised money by selling shares to investors, which spread the risk of expensive voyages, and it was allowed to wage war, make treaties, and build forts.

The VOC took Portuguese strongholds in the Indian Ocean, founded Batavia on Java in 1619 as its Asian headquarters, and controlled much of the spice trade by forcing growers in places such as the Banda Islands to sell only to the company. By the late 1600s, Amsterdam was one of the leading financial centers of Europe.

questions.explanation: The passage says the company was granted powers to wage war, make treaties, and build forts.
choiceExplanations: The passage describes no tax on voters in the Netherlands.
The company traded in Asia and did not appoint Dutch officials.
The passage says the company was granted powers to wage war, make treaties, and build forts.
The VOC did not write laws for other nations' merchants.
questions.distinguisher: The company had the power to rule in its territories, but not to govern the Dutch state.
